# Outline — what the paper says and what carries it (revision 1)

Source: `idea-repo` Brief revision 4 (the idea, the predictions P1–P5, the study design and cell budget), the objective (`story-repo`#1) and `prior_work.md`. This page says *what to test and where it shows*, never what a result must be. Every claim below has a "refuted if" line; a result that triggers it changes the claim, and I take it to `idea-repo` (see "When results do not carry it").

## 1. The story in one paragraph
Regression-adjustment estimators of the global average treatment effect (GATE) under network interference (Chin 2019; Han–Ugander 2023) fit outcome on functions of the assignment (own treatment, treated-neighbour fraction, …) and predict at all-treated and all-control. Published work shows they *can* work but gives no account of *how well, why, and when not*. We treat the estimator as **extrapolation from the observed exposure distribution to the two global corners** and ask what that predicts. The error splits into a **variance part** (OLS leverage of the corner contrast, scaling like d/(p(1−p)n)) and a **bias part** (curvature of the response × raw distance of the corner from the observed exposure support, roughly *not* growing with degree). The two parts have different drivers and can move in opposite directions with degree, so "error grows with degree" is true only where noise dominates. We test these scalings across interference mechanisms, graph families (synthetic and two real Facebook graphs), treatment probabilities and designs (Bernoulli, graph-cluster); map where regression beats and loses to difference-in-means (DM) and to exposure-mapping HT/Hájek; ask whether flexible/data-adaptive learners help; and test a data-computable two-part diagnostic against pre-registered trivial predictors. Not a new estimator: a verified, predictive account of when to trust an existing one. Positive, negative and mixed outcomes are all reported.

## 2. Position against prior work (Related work, one paragraph per cluster)
- *Regression GATE estimators*: Chin 2019 (estimator; Fig. 2 already shows the exposure-distribution mismatch qualitatively and draws the off-policy analogy), Han–Ugander 2023 (covariate generation/selection, block bootstrap). **We do not claim the extrapolation viewpoint as new**; we claim the quantified decomposition, its tests across mechanisms/graphs/designs, the regime map including where regression loses, and the diagnostic. - *Misspecification / unknown interference*: Sävje et al. 2021, Leung 2022, Sävje 2023, Yu et al. 2022 — our setting is estimand = GATE with a possibly wrong response model.
- *Designs*: Karrer et al. 2021, Cortez et al. 2022 (optional), Chen et al. 2023, Leung 2022 rate. *Overlap/positivity*: Crump 2009, D'Amour 2021 (where the extrapolation analogy comes from).

1	# Brief — idea of the study (revision 4, after idea-review round 2)
2	
3	## Question
4	With network interference, how accurate is the regression-based GATE estimator (fit outcome on functions of the assignment vector — own treatment, treated-neighbour fraction/count, higher-order terms — then predict at all-treated and all-control and difference; Chin 2019, Han & Ugander 2023)? What determines its error, and under which interference mechanisms, networks and designs does it hold, fail, or lose to the biased difference in means?
5	
6	## Thesis (the claim the paper is built around)
7	The regression GATE estimator is limited by **extrapolation from the observed exposure distribution to the global-treatment and global-control corners**, and the two parts of its error — variance and bias — have *different* drivers that move in opposite directions with degree. A data-computable two-part diagnostic separates them and tells an experimenter when to trust the estimate, when a flexible learner cannot rescue it, and when the biased DM is the better choice. The extrapolation viewpoint itself is not new (Chin 2019 shows the feature distributions at global treatment/control differ from the observed one and invokes off-policy evaluation, qualitatively); the claimed contribution is the quantified, tested account, its interaction with the design, and the regime map including where regression loses.
8	
9	### Notation
10	Features φ_i(z) (own z_i; treated-neighbour fraction f_i; optional count, 2-hop, interaction terms). τ̂ = Δxᵀβ̂ with Δx = mean_i[φ_i(1) − φ_i(0)] (the intercept cancels). Corner offsets: raw exposure distances of the corners from the observed exposure distribution, (1−p) for all-treated and p for all-control (fraction feature; mechanism-specific for count/2-hop).
11	
12	### Predictions (fixed now; each falsifiable)
13	**Variance part.**
14	- *Leverage* L = Δxᵀ Σ̂_φ⁻¹ Δx, Σ̂_φ the empirical covariance of the feature rows under the observed assignment (pooled primary; the per-unit average of per-unit leverage is reported as variant for heterogeneous degree). For the fraction feature, L ≈ (1+d)/(p(1−p)) for features (own z, f), i.e. ∝ d/(p(1−p)) at large d; minimal at p = ½.
15	- P1. Where residuals are independent with variance σ², Var(τ̂) ≈ σ² L / n (OLS leverage; textbook, stated as the baseline, not the finding). The test is the *departure*: fit log-RMSE on log n, log d, log p(1−p) with CIs, on graphs where the iid formula is expected to hold (ER/SBM, Bernoulli) and where not (BA hubs, cluster designs, degree-correlated baselines, 2-hop features with shared neighbours); report where σ²L/n over- or under-states the realised variance and by what factor (an effective-n). Noise model fixed: iid Gaussian ε with σ a multiple of the SD of the noise-free outcome ({0.25,0.5,1}), plus unit baselines a_i that are iid or degree/community-correlated; with σ=0 and correct spec the error is exactly 0 and such cells serve only as a sanity check.
16	**Bias part.**
17	- P2. For a response g(f) curved in exposure and a linear fit tangent near p, spillover bias ≈ −½g''(1−2p) to second order (zero at p = ½), plus a third-order term −(1/6)g'''[(1−p)³+p³]; it depends on *raw* distance × curvature and **not** on d (large d only narrows the observed support, so the bias neither grows nor shrinks with d for the fraction feature). # Prior work and how the study relates to it

Keys refer to `prior_work.bib`. Only entries checked on 2026-11-25 are listed. The papers' details beyond the abstracts have not all been read; the report role should read a source before attributing a specific theorem to it.

## Closest work (the study must be positioned against these)

The study uses it as the primary object. Open: no systematic account of when its error is large, no comparison across interference forms, network families and designs, no data-computable warning.
- **Han & Ugander 2023** (`han2023model`): model-based regression adjustment with generated graph/treatment covariates, block-bootstrap CIs, semi-synthetic and real checks. Baseline (richer covariate set) and the closest competitor for "which features". Open: the error is not explained by a quantity that can be computed before/after the experiment.
- What the full texts of Chin 2019, Han–Ugander 2023 and Gao–Ding 2023 say (read 2026-11-25 by keyword and section, not in full): Chin (Fig. 2) already shows that the treated-neighbour fraction/count distributions under one observed Bernoulli(0.5) draw differ from those under global treatment/control, draws the off-policy-evaluation analogy, requires an exogeneity (correct-response-model) assumption, and says extrapolation "may not be too unreasonable" if the response is low-dimensional — qualitative, no scaling in degree/p/design. Han–Ugander note that the variance of sample means of the features may not scale as 1/n and give bias/RMSE tables over feature sets. Gao–Ding assume overlap of exposure probabilities and study regression estimators of exposure-mapping estimands (not GATE extrapolation). So the extrapolation viewpoint is not new; the quantified account, its decomposition, the design interaction and the diagnostic are the claimed additions, "to our knowledge within the literature checked".
- **Gao & Ding 2023** (`gao2023causal`): regression-based analysis of network experiments with design-based properties. Closest design-based treatment of regression estimators; to be read in detail before the paper states what is new.
